Pele Yoetz 178:2: And it is true that it is fitting for a person to cast his burden upon the LORD, and he must settle his mind at the time he is engaged in Torah or in prayer, and even if he has many troubles and evils worse than the evils of Job, nothing should distract him from the service of the blessed Name, as it is written (Deuteronomy 6:5), "and you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot 61b): even if He takes your soul. But who among men would do this and who among men would hold fast to it? Would that we serve our Creator with complete service when we have no trouble at all, for the nearby inclination confuses our minds with foreign thoughts and vanity of vanities, and when we have any trouble at all, we are like drunkards and our service is turbid and we cannot direct our minds. Therefore an obligation rests upon us to minimize, as much as we can, our troubles in order to serve our Creator with perfect service - such a thing, perhaps.
Pele Yoetz 178:3: And likewise, a settled mind is a great necessity for engagement in Torah so that one can examine and direct his mind toward its truth and dwell in the depth of halachah. And happy is whoever can fix his study in a place designated for himself alone, so that the voice of children and household members not distract him. And it is included in this that a person be settled in all his affairs, whether in study or in the service of the blessed Name or in worldly matters, for "the fruit of haste is regret" (Mivchar HaPeninim 43:27), and deliberateness is worth four hundred zuz (Berachot 20a).
Pele Yoetz 179:1: Letter Kaf: Honoring Father and Mother - It is known that the obligation of their honor is great, for Scripture has equated their honor with the honor of the Omnipresent (Kiddushin 30b), and whoever treats their honor with contempt, his sin is great. And now, because of our sins, unrestrained sons have multiplied, and it seems light in their eyes not to honor father and mother, but rather they increase transgressing against their mind - and there are corrupt sons who treat their honor with contempt and cause them soul-pain and set their parents' teeth on edge. And especially the man who fears the LORD, who greatly desires His mitzvot and disciplines his sons, and they do not heed his voice and anger him to his face - this man's pain is great, for bad upbringing within his own house is difficult, and his teeth shall grind and melt, and it is bitter, bitter to him. Woe to sons who cause this to their fathers, alas for them, woe upon them. Woe to them from the day of judgment, for God shall bring everything into judgment - for what he transgressed against the mind of his Maker, and what he transgressed against the mind of his father and mother and distressed them, and for having caused anger to his father as a foolish son, and for embittering his own mother's life - while he enjoys the fruits in this world, so shall his own sons do to him, for measure for measure has not been nullified, and the principal remains for the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 179:2: And it is true that the obligation of honoring father and mother is very severe, to the point that not every person can fulfill his obligation properly, so that the sages of the Talmud said (ibid. 31b): happy is he who has not known them - yet every person is obligated to do whatever is in his power to do with all his strength, and should not despair, for although they said (ibid. 32a) that a father who forgoes his own honor, his honor is forgone - and certainly this is the trait of every person, that he forgoes his honor toward his sons - nevertheless he is punished by the laws of Heaven for having transgressed the saying of the Merciful One. Go out and learn from our elder father Jacob, peace be upon him, what befell him for the twenty-two years he did not serve his father (Megillah 17a). And Joseph the righteous had his years shortened because he heard them say to him, "your servant our father," and remained silent (Sotah 13b). And all the more so, disgrace and distress caused to them are not forgiven, for the pain of the body is not something one can forgo.
Pele Yoetz 179:3: Behold, therefore, beloved young men, worthy sons of Israel, give honor to your God and be careful of the honor of your father and your mother, and do not turn from what they command you, right or left, even if they tell you that right is left - for this is a bad, sick trait found in sons who cannot be trusted, that they consider themselves wiser and more understanding than their father and mother. If only they were wise, they would understand that the Torah has testified that wisdom is with the aged and understanding with length of days (Job 12:12). And it is written (Proverbs 12:15): "the way of a fool is straight in his own eyes." And the Tanna said (Avot 4:14): "and do not lean on your own understanding." And even if it were as they say, that their father and mother lack knowledge, God forbid, the decree of the Almighty stands over them to heed their voice and not anger them, even if, in their own opinion, they act toward them improperly and not as is proper. This is the statute of the Torah, for they said (Kiddushin 31a[?]): how far does honoring father and mother extend? To the point that if he takes his own purse in his presence and throws it into the sea, he shall not embarrass him.
Pele Yoetz 179:4: And I have already stated that there are mitzvot dependent on luck [i.e., opportunity], for how much money a person spends to perform the mitzvah of opening the ark, or to be a sandak, and the like, even though there is neither a Torah-mandated mitzvah nor a Rabbinic one, only a cherishing of a mitzvah in general - happy is Israel, for every single time he heeds the voice of his father and his mother, he fulfills a great Torah-mandated mitzvah, and fools transgress it and are punished.
Pele Yoetz 179:5: And it is fitting for a wise son to rejoice at his father and desire that he command him something in order to do it and fulfill a Torah-mandated mitzvah. And even if it is burdensome for him and the nearby inclination incites him doubly, let him incite the good inclination against the evil inclination and bear it and not grow weary and not delay doing whatever comes from his mouth, lest another beat him to it. And according to the pain is the reward, and he enjoys the fruits in this world of having worthy sons - for even if this were the only reward, it would be enough to labor with his twenty fingernails to merit this. And the entire aim of an understanding son shall be to know his father's will in order to do it and give peace of mind to his Father in Heaven. And if the son is graced by the LORD with wealth and his father is a poor man, an obligation rests upon him to support him and supply all his needs with a pleasant countenance and words of appeasement, in a manner of honor. And if he has members of his household, let him instruct them all with all firmness to be careful of their honor. And there are sons who are on good terms with their father and mother until they marry a wife, but once they marry, the daughter-in-law rises up against her mother-in-law and incites her husband to make a quarrel. And the God-fearing man who desires life shall rebuke his wife and silence her with a reproach to put his father's and mother's minds at ease, and afterward appease her privately, between himself and her, and rebuke her and guide her on the straight path - this is the straight path.
Pele Yoetz 179:6: And the essence of the honor is that he honor them at their death, and let him do daily, without forgetting, whatever is in his power to do to give rest to their souls - not like many of the common people who remember their father and mother only briefly on the yahrzeit day, saying Kaddish and giving a little charity and studying a little. Woe to the fathers who expect their sons to redeem them and raise them up from the pit of destruction, when what they do accomplishes almost nothing either way - and would that it not detract, as many of the common people do, who say the Kaddish hastily, and likewise the blessings of the Haftarah, and errors, who can understand - to the point that their blessings are in vain, and likewise when they wish to pray with the congregation, to the point that I am concerned that instead of "delight" for their fathers, they cause "affliction," God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 179:7: Behold, therefore, it is fitting for the son who honors his father to recognize his own place, and not rely on himself to say Kaddishes and Haftarahs and prayers until he first goes to a sage and has him examine him - and if he is not fit for this, it is better that he hire some Torah scholar to study and say Kaddishes and pray for the rest of his father's and mother's souls. And he should not do this only for the twelve months and the day of the twelfth month, and afterward rest and stand for his own lot - one must be concerned about this, and all the more so since the saying of Kaddishes is not only to save from punishment, but also causes an elevation for the soul of the deceased. Behold, therefore, it is fitting for the son that all the days of his life his father's image be engraved on his face, and he shall imagine as though he were crying out bitterly from within a flame of fire, saying, "my son, my beloved, be gracious to me, be gracious to me, save my soul from the sword, my only one from the hand of the dog" (Psalms 22:21). And even if he thinks his father is a complete righteous man and his soul delights in fatness, he shall imagine as though he were giving him delicacies as his father loved, in order that his soul bless him - and therefore let him not fail even one day, all the days of his life, to say Kaddish and give charity for the soul of his parents. And how good it would be for him to have it fluent in his mouth to say every single day:
Pele Yoetz 179:8: May it be Your will, LORD our God and God of our fathers, that You accept with mercy and favor every good deed that I do, whether in thought, in speech, or in deed, and let it all be for the merit, the rest, and the elevation of the nefesh, ruach, and neshamah of my father and my mother and my father-in-law and my mother-in-law, and so on. May it be Your will that his soul be bound in the bond of life.
Pele Yoetz 179:9: And through this he shall carry a blessing from the LORD and from the soul of his parents. And happy is the man who does not depend on his sons' table, and fulfills the verse (Psalms 49:19), "and they praise you when you do well for yourself." And he shall not leave all his wealth to others, but let his own righteousness go before him. And well known is the parable of the candle, which gives light forward and not backward - and let some of it remain from his sons, but only as a surplus.
Pele Yoetz 179:10: And included in honoring father and mother is to strive with all vigor to bring merit to their souls by sending them to the Land of Israel, and even if their separation and their expense are difficult for him, everything is as nothing compared to the peace of mind he gives them by bringing merit to their souls, and through this he shall be reconciled for having sinned against them. And since our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Kiddushin 31b), "happy is he who has not known them," for he cannot fulfill his obligation - but when he is not with them, so that the evil inclination does not incite him, his soul desires to honor them with great vigor and might, and a good thought the Holy One, blessed be He, joins to the deed - for this too it is good to send them to the Land of Israel.
Pele Yoetz 179:11: And since our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 8a) that a person should not dwell near his teacher where it is not pleasant for him, we learn from this that if a person cannot honor father and mother as is proper, if the LORD has graced him with the ability to support himself, it is better that he not be dependent on his father's table, if it is his father's own will. And likewise it is good for a man, if possible for him, to separate his sons from his own table, so as not to transgress "before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block" (Leviticus 19:14), and there shall be peace in his tent. And it is found in Tanna D'vei Eliyahu (Rabbah, ch. 26): "honor your father," and adjacent to it, "you shall not commit adultery" - to teach you that if he marries a wife and she does not honor his father and mother, it is as though he committed adultery all his days. Therefore he must go out to meet combat, to fight with his wife within, for the honor of his father and mother. But the yoke also hangs upon the father and mother, not to cause division and hatred between a man and his wife, God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 180:1: Honoring the Wise - Great is the honor of the wise, as explained in the Talmud and the Holy Zohar, and all this applies to the entire people through inadvertence - for Torah scholars withhold their hands from preaching this in the assembly of the people, lest people say they preach for their own honor. But it is fitting for the wise to accord honor to their colleagues, for they said (Shabbat 34a): harlots adorn one another - Torah scholars, all the more so! And it is not only that Torah scholars stand before one another and accord honor among themselves, but even for whoever is beginning in the ways of study, it is fitting even for a great sage to accord him honor, for two reasons: one, so that others see and do likewise, and furthermore, in order to make the Torah beloved to its students, when they see the praise of the Torah, "for whoever finds it finds life" (Proverbs 8:35), righteousness and honor.
Pele Yoetz 180:2: And the man whom the LORD has graced with understanding and who knows what the Torah said (Leviticus 19:32), "you shall rise before gray hair" or before a Torah scholar, fulfills a Torah-mandated mitzvah, and his reward is abundant and great, for he merits the fear of Heaven (Bamidbar Rabbah 15:17), as the disciples of the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote. And now many of the common people are not concerned to rise either before gray hair or before a Torah scholar, for they do not know what this is - may the good LORD atone for this. And of such a case they said (Kiddushin 33a): whoever goes around lives longer - in order not to transgress "before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block." But if he sees that mitzvot are dear to them and it is not burdensome for them to rise, let him pass before them so that they fulfill the mitzvah and receive reward, and that there be peace of mind before our Father in Heaven according to how they regard him - for even if they are mistaken about him, in any case he performs a mitzvah and it is beneficial to give peace of mind above. And beforehand let him take it to heart and say thus: "I know of myself that I am not worthy, and my own sins shall be smelled by my neighbors, and I shall know my own transgression," and the like, so that his heart not become haughty and he not enjoy the honor, for it is known what is written in Sefer Chasidim (siman 8), that whatever a person enjoys in this world of the honor accorded to him is deducted from his merits.
Pele Yoetz 180:3: And included in this honor, toward everyone entitled to it - such as his father and mother, a Torah scholar, and the synagogue - is that he should not speak even with others in their presence in a loud voice, and needless to say he should not disparage or curse them in their presence, for it turns out that he does not value them and does not fear them as he would fear the government, and it is as though he disparages them. Therefore all his words in their presence shall be in a low voice and in a manner of honor and proper conduct - not only toward them, but even toward others in their presence - not like many of the common people who, when standing in judgment before the judge, raise their voices with a mighty voice and disparage and curse one another with great insolence, worse than in a butcher shop or a tavern. Woe to that shame, woe to that disgrace - let them see how, when standing before our enemies who judge us, there is no voice and no answer, and "let not the priestess be like the innkeeper's wife" (Yevamot 122a). Whoever is God-fearing, it is fitting for him to subdue his anger, and even if his fellow stirs up strife and speaks foolishly with many words, let him not answer the fool according to his folly (Proverbs 26:4), but rather guard a muzzle upon his mouth for the honor of the Torah. And even if there are only three laymen, such as in our time, let him stand before them with awe and honor out of fear of the LORD, who judges among the judges, and even if it seems to him that they have treated him improperly, let him not curse God, but believe that judgment belongs to God, and God is the judge. And this suffices for whoever has a good heart and sound understanding.
Pele Yoetz 181:1: The Honor of Creatures - Great is the honor of creatures, which overrides a negative commandment of the Torah (Berachot 19b). And well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Kallah, ch. 4[?]): honor every person as Rabban Gamliel and suspect them as robbers. And well known is the saying of the sage, who would say that it is fitting to honor every person: if he is wiser than me, it is fitting to honor him for his wisdom; and if I am wiser than him, it turns out that he is more righteous than me, for I sin willfully and he sins inadvertently. If he is rich, it is fitting to honor him for his wealth, for the great men of Israel, Rabbi and Rabbi Akiva, would honor the wealthy (Eruvin 86a), for the King desires his honor. And if I am rich and he is poor, it turns out that I sin, for I do not perform charity as I should, and he is righteous in this. And they said in the Talmud (Pesachim 113b): whoever knows about his fellow that he has one good quality more than himself is obligated to accord him honor.
Pele Yoetz 181:2: And I recall having seen in the Midrash that it is fitting to honor the poor man and rise before him for the honor of the blessed Name, as it is written (Psalms 109:31): "for He stands at the right hand of the needy." And well known is the saying of the Tanna (Avot 4:1): who is honored? He who honors creatures. And he further said (ibid.): do not be scornful of any person. And whoever accords honor to the rich and treats the poor's honor lightly does not do well, for the LORD shall contend their cause and demand their disgrace, for their distress is great, and they complain about the ways of the Holy One, blessed be He. And when a person makes a feast and invites his guests, how good and how pleasant it would be for the rich and the poor to recline at one table, for through this they are honored. And likewise, every rich man who shows a smiling face to a poor man and speaks with him and accords him honor - it shall be counted a great mitzvah for him, for he revives the heart of the downtrodden and gladdens the heart of the wretched. And especially if his own relatives are destitute poor, let him not be ashamed to show that they are his relatives, but rather draw his relatives near and visit them at their celebrations and on festivals - this is his own honor.
Pele Yoetz 181:3: And it is fitting for a person to have within him something of the knowledge of his Maker, that He cherishes the poor and visits them. And it is written (Isaiah 57:15): "I dwell with the crushed." And it is known that a person's own will is his honor, and it is fitting to get to the bottom of everyone's mind and do his will, and nullify his own will before the will of others. And they have already told of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, that it once happened that a certain Torah scholar did not know him and wished to walk before him, while he himself intended to walk behind him in order to do his will and honor him. And let him reason a fortiori from this incident on that day: all the more so is it fitting to be careful with the honor of the King of honor.
Pele Yoetz 182:1: Anger - Well known is the severity of anger; how strict they were about it in the Talmud and the Holy Zohar and the writings of the Ari, of blessed memory - it makes one's hair stand on end. And according to its severity, the man who desires life and has the nature and trait of anger shall muster his strength with great vigor and might to make fences and hedges for himself to restrain himself and save his own soul from descending to the pit, and shall wage war with stratagems not to come to a state of anger. And the great fence is that he write down and gather all the sayings of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in the Talmud, Midrashim, the Holy Zohar, and the words of the Ari, of blessed memory, and let them be a remembrance in his eyes, and let him meditate on them every single day so that he fear and be afraid and draw back and incite the good inclination against the evil inclination - if it helps, good; and if not, let him fine himself each time he becomes angry with money or fasts. And if he cannot restrain his own spirit from becoming angry, in any case let him guard a muzzle on his mouth from speaking, whether for good or evil, at the time of his anger, and be as one deaf who does not hear and as one mute who does not open his mouth. And if he speaks, let it be in a low voice and with placating words, and even if his heart burns like fire and his wrath burns within him, let him restrain it with words - then the anger shall be essentially bearing no fruit, for it is known that a transgression of anger drags many bad transgressions along with it, such as the fire of division, and he shall be clothed in a curse, and many such evils - and silence at a time of anger is like water to fire. And well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Chullin 89a), on the verse "He hangs the earth on nothing" (Job 26:7), that the world endures only for the sake of whoever restrains his mouth at a time of quarrel.
Pele Yoetz 182:2: And let him take to heart how he can be angry at another who has repaid him with evil, and not be angry at himself for causing evil to his own soul, consuming himself from soul to flesh with his own anger. And let him consider what he is and what his life is, and that honor and disgrace and all worldly matters are all vanity, vanity of vanities, a work of delusion, and that a person does not stub his own finger below unless it is decreed upon him from above (Chullin 7b), and what does a living man complain, a man about his own sins? And that a person does not touch what is prepared for his fellow, and that the way of a fool is straight in his own eyes, and there is no reason to blame him and be angry - let him remove anger from his heart and put away evil from his flesh. And if the beginning is distressing until he becomes accustomed to it, in the end the habit becomes a good nature for him. And it is not praiseworthy for one who has no reason to be angry and nothing to be angry about, and is not angry - rather, the obligation of a man is that even if he has sufficient reason to be angry, he shall subdue his anger. And if he needs to cast harshness upon his sons and the like, he shall do so only outwardly. And if it happens that he becomes angry, let him be quick to be appeased for the honor of his Maker, and through this he shall be satisfied and full of the LORD's blessing, and even his own flesh shall dwell securely.
Pele Yoetz 183:1: Intention - It is known that the intention of the heart is the essential matter, and this is a great principle in the service of the blessed Name. Regarding mitzvot dependent on speech, they said (Abravanel, Avot 2:13): prayer without intention is like a body without a soul. And regarding mitzvot dependent on action, they said (Berachot 13a): mitzvot require intention. And come and see how great is the power of intention, to the point that they said (Nazir 23b): greater is a transgression for its own sake than a mitzvah not for its own sake. Of this it is said (Hosea 14:10): "for the ways of the LORD are straight, and the righteous shall walk in them, but the transgressors shall stumble in them," as they explained in the Talmud (Nazir 23a). And one mitzvah draws another, for according to the greatness of the intention, so shall fear, love, cleaving, desire, affection, and exactingness in the mitzvot increase, to perform them in all their details, their proper forms, and their fine points. And it is true that our sins withhold the good from us, and they are the screens that separate between us and our Father in Heaven, to the point that we cannot direct our minds to serve our Creator with complete and perfect service, as is proper to do, and also the troubles and incidents of the time confuse our minds. And they have already said in the Talmud (Eruvin 65a) that Rav Sheshet said: I could exempt the whole world from the law of prayer, as it is written (Isaiah 51:21), "and drunk, but not with wine" - in any case, he is destined to give a judgment and reckoning for not having striven with great vigor and might, and for what was in his power to do and he did not do, to intend at least from time to time in some blessing or some prayer, or even in some word going back and forth, or in some mitzvah - for everything joins and adds to the reckoning, for this is part of the mercies and kindnesses of God, blessed be His Name, as the Kabbalists have written: that if a person intends on one day in one blessing and on another day in another blessing, the Holy One, blessed be He, joins them together, until a complete prayer with intention is made, which ascends to be a crown of glory upon the head of the righteous who lives forever.
Pele Yoetz 184:1: Honor - We learned (Avot 4:21): jealousy, desire, and honor remove a person from the world. And the reason is that each of these brings many companion evils along with it, which consume from soul to flesh. For whoever pursues honor, all his days are pains, for his entire aim, desire, and will is that people honor him, and he labors to grow rich and spends much on matters of honor, and if at some time they do not honor him, or do something to him that, in his own opinion, is not befitting his honor or is contempt for his honor, his own flesh grieves over him, and if he can, he makes quarrel and strife, and a flame of division rises to the heart of heaven. And all the divisions in the world come only from pride, for one wishes to rise in his own pride to the skies, and thinks that honor befits and is fitting for him, and that his word shall not return empty - and toward whoever treats his honor with contempt and does not heed his word, he takes vengeance and bears a grudge like a serpent, and does whatever evil he can to him. And if he cannot do anything to him, in any case he complains against him and hates his brother in his heart, and his hatred, which teaches eternal enmity, shall be seen - he becomes angry, his teeth grind and melt because he cannot do anything, until he descends in mourning to the grave. This is his punishment in this world, and in the World to Come all the more so, for the pursuit of honor does not go forth to teach about itself alone, but it is the offspring of impurity from pride, and it has offspring and offspring's offspring of impurity - what comes forth from the impure is impure.
Pele Yoetz 184:2: And it is fitting for a person to flee from honor as one flees from fire, for it is a fire that consumes unto destruction. And regarding every bad trait that a person's inclination desires and covets, one must strengthen himself with great vigor and might, with pure thoughts, to distance himself from them, for the punishment of bad traits is harsh, especially these things that remove a person from the world. And let him consider and say: what am I and what is my life - a putrid drop, dust and ashes, worm and maggot, a vessel full of excrement, shame and disgrace, and what are we - a thing without substance? And what does it give me and what does it add for me if men like myself honor me or disgrace me - I and they are vanity of vanities? And if I honor before the King of honor, what do I care about the imagined honor of men? And if I am despised and disgraceful before the King of honor and all the host of on high, why do I need life and why do I need honor from men? Let the day I was born perish. And it is likely that I am a sinner, despised above, for if I were worthy of honor, they would have granted me honor from Heaven - but certainly I am a sinner, and my sins withhold honor from me, and the LORD said to him, "curse." Over this let his heart be humbled and let him accept the judgment of Heaven with joy, and not complain against any person and not quarrel with any person, for what does a living man complain, a man about his own sins?
Pele Yoetz 184:3: And another principle: let him judge every person favorably (Avot 1:6). For the man whose way is straight in his own eyes acts to the extent his own understanding reaches, and what more could he have done - could he have acquired his fellow's own mind to get to the bottom of his understanding and do his will as he wishes? Behold, therefore, one should not blame anyone for anything, for the way of a man is straight in his own eyes - rather, let us ask our God, from the womb, to set us right with good counsel from before Him. And not only is it not fitting to pursue honor, for its evil is great and shall come to confusion - for such is the trait, that whoever pursues honor, honor flees from him (see Shevet Musar, ch. 17) - but even if they accord him honor, let him flee from honor as from a sword, for he is very prone to stumble and be an abomination to the LORD, any amount of haughtiness of heart, if he goes out to meet combat to subdue his inclination not to enjoy the honor. Therefore it is better to flee if he can, and he should not consider
Pele Yoetz 184:4: himself worthy of honor while fleeing from it, so that honor pursue him - for this is the humble man who has put on arrogance, and his hope is dashed, that honor shall not pursue him, but rather it shall flee in spirit.
Pele Yoetz 184:5: But the obligation is to be truly humble, and to believe with complete faith that he is not worthy of any honor in the world, according to the greatness of his own lowliness and poverty, his own small worth and limited grasp, and the very essence of his sins. And if the world errs about him and honors him, this shall add to his own grief, for he shall be sated with disgrace instead of honor in the World to Come, and his heart shall tremble within him, saying, "my sins shall be smelled by my neighbors, they shall distance themselves from me and from my borders." And even if it seems to him that there are those lower, worse, and more sinful than himself, he should not seek greatness and should not covet honor from them, for the scale and just balances are in the hand of the LORD, and every person is judged according to his own grasp, knowledge, and ability, and according to the abundance of his good fortune, so does his obligation increase, in a manner that "he who adds knowledge adds sorrow" (Ecclesiastes 1:18), lest he has not done what he should have done - and let him consider that in the scale of the sanctuary, certainly his fellow is greater than him and he is lesser, more despised than all creatures, with none like him below. This is a great principle for being saved from everything evil and for fleeing from honor in this world, and thereby he shall behold the vision of the Almighty. However, for whoever is a leader of the community, it is fitting to be somewhat exacting about his own honor outwardly, so that his fear rest upon the community. There is a time to act for the LORD, a time for every desire - everything depends on the need. Good is patience, and if it seems to him that he must take revenge, let him take revenge and bear a grudge like a serpent for the sake of Heaven, and everything with scale and balances, and sound understanding sevenfold.
Pele Yoetz 185:1: Yom Kippur - Yom Kippur is a mighty day among the days of the year, and happy is Israel, all of whom are aroused on these mighty days, and especially on the Day of Atonement, for the LORD looks down from heaven upon the children of men and places in their hearts fear of the great and awesome judgment and arousal to repentance. And would that their hearts remain thus all the days! But they have already said (Berachot 33b) that everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven - only through the LORD's compassion for His people Israel, the people close to Him, does He shine His face upon them on these mighty days with the light of fear and dread, and from the splendor of the abundance of these days it shall be drawn to a person for the whole year. And according to how he is aroused on these mighty days, and strengthens himself to fear the LORD, and makes fences and hedges for himself, and accepts upon himself to conduct himself even after Yom Kippur in the ways of repentance, so shall he find help corresponding to it for the whole year to fear the LORD, and the pure fear of the LORD endures forever (Psalms 19:10), and he shall rise in levels until he is purified of his impurity and finds the means of his own redemption.
Pele Yoetz 185:2: Behold, because of our sins, we have acted foolishly, and no man regrets his own evil - only on these mighty days do people become somewhat careful in the ways of solitary devotion, rising early at the watches for selichot, and the people increase somewhat in studying Psalms and other studies, and on Rosh Hashanah day they perform the Tashlich order and say, "we have already cast our sins into the water," and on the eve of Yom Kippur they perform kapparot, and on Yom Kippur they sit in the synagogue all day and read the words of the prayers in a loud voice, and their cry rises until the earth would split at their voice. And if it happens to them, even on that day, to speak in the synagogue, or to be exacting and make division, and similar bad and forbidden things, they do not abandon their custom, for they cannot restrain themselves to subdue their own inclination.
Pele Yoetz 185:3: And many of the common people are not careful with the affliction of washing, for they wash their faces and hands up to the wrist every day, and are not careful with the affliction of wearing shoes, for they do not remove their shoes except when they come to their place in the synagogue - and it turns out that on the day of forgiveness they add transgression to their sin, thinking that they have already fulfilled their obligation and been purified of all their iniquities and all their sins. Would that the LORD say so and count the little as much! And may the good LORD atone for this, for the whole people acts inadvertently and does not know what the straight path is, but rather the custom of their fathers is in their hands, a mitzvah of men learned by rote. And what shall the son do who does not know which way light dwells, and night is as bright as day for him, darkness as light, and he thinks, "what else is my obligation, that I might do it?" On whom shall we lean? On our Father in Heaven - He, in His mercy, shall shine His face upon us forever and bless us all with the light of His face, for in the light of the king's face is life.
Pele Yoetz 185:4: However, "the Jews had light" - this is Torah, and this is its reward: whoever meditates on it shall attain the way of life and shall keep the paths of the righteous, for according to what is explained in the words of the Sages, our holy Rabbis, this is not the way that removes a person from transgression. And it is already explained through Isaiah the prophet (58:4-7) in the Haftarah read on Yom Kippur, where he says: "behold, you fast for strife and contention, and to strike with a wicked fist. You shall not fast as you do today, to make your voice heard on high. Is such the fast I choose, a day for a man to afflict his soul? Is it to bow his head like a bulrush? Will you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the LORD? Is not this the fast I choose: to loosen the bonds of wickedness," and so on. "Is it not to share your bread with the hungry," and so on. And so it is explained in the words of the prophets (ibid. 55:7): "let the wicked forsake his way, and the man of iniquity his thoughts, and let him return to the LORD, and He shall have mercy on him." And it is written (Proverbs 28:14): "and whoever acknowledges and forsakes shall find mercy." And many such holy scriptures in the words of the prophets teach the ways of repentance.
Pele Yoetz 185:5: And it is likewise explained in all the holy books - Talmud, Midrashim, Holy Zohar, and books of ethics - that it is true that the inherent virtue of Yom Kippur is to restrain transgression and bring sin to an end, and He acquits those who repent but does not acquit those who do not repent, for there are four categories of atonement: repentance and Yom Kippur, suffering, and death - all according to what the sin is. And how many repairs and orders of fasts and mortifications have been stated for the sinning soul, from the holy mouth of the master, the Ari, and other holy men, for every iniquity and every sin. And if Yom Kippur alone sufficed, all this would not be necessary, for Yom Kippur passes over us always, year after year. And granted that Yom Kippur is beneficial and performs purification even for those who do not repent, for it is the day that causes it, being effective for this - but it performs only a minor purification, and when, after Yom Kippur, one returns to his evil ways, everything returns to its original state.
Pele Yoetz 185:6: And our teacher, the Rabbi Rabbi Yehonatan, has already written in the book Ya'arot Devash, that when the husk sees in a person that there is no impression of holiness in him because he increases impurity and guilt, and the husk finds no moisture of holiness in him to suck from him, what does it do? It puts it in his heart to increase somewhat, on the mighty days, in mitzvot and good deeds temporarily, not with the intention of persisting in this - and this is bad for him, for when he afterward returns to his evil ways, all the mitzvot and good deeds he performed fall into the portion of the predator; the Other Side has swallowed the wealth. Of such a case it is said (Psalms 50:16): "and to the wicked, God says, what right have you to declare My statutes," and so on. And from this he goes from evil to evil, and the sinning soul, it shall die in its sin, for the way of a man is straight in his own eyes; even when he grows old he shall not depart from it. And even if he hears words of ethics and rebuke during the year, they do not arouse the heart, for their eyes are plastered from seeing, their hearts from understanding, and their sins are separating screens blinding the perceptive, in a manner that they walk in darkness forever and shall not see light, until they descend in mourning to the grave, and the fault causes the delay of the Messiah for these many long years, years many and evil. Woe to us for the day of judgment and woe to us for the day of rebuke. But whoever is the man who desires life and wishes to have regard for the honor of his Maker and for his own nefesh, ruach, and neshamah - our Former has already instructed us to choose the way, the way of life, as it is written (Deuteronomy 30:19), "and you shall choose life." And this is the way of the upright, God-fearing man: he shall not wait until the mighty days and Yom Kippur to be aroused, but rather every single day shall be in his eyes like Yom Kippur, and all his days shall be in repentance. Happy is the man who is always fearful.
Pele Yoetz 185:7: However, whoever did not set his heart during the days of his vain life, and walked in darkness with no light for him, and spent his days in vanity and his years in confusion as is the way of the world, behold, when the time of the mighty days arrives, if he merits that his eyes be opened and light shine upon him, this shall be his practice, which shall benefit to revive him: that he increase in studying or hearing teachings of words of ethics and fear of the LORD, which pierce the heart to its innermost chamber, and with his eyes he shall see, and with his ears he shall hear, and his heart shall understand that it is bad and bitter that they have forsaken the LORD, and he shall be embittered with great bitterness and regret completely for everything he did that was not good, and for everything he sinned against his own soul, and for having caused many evils and distress to Heaven through his sins - and during these days he shall minimize his business, even the business of study, and shall engage in books of ethics with the intention of keeping, doing, and fulfilling, and shall desire with a whole heart and a willing soul to repair his own flaws and walk in the way of the good, and shall inquire from a book, from the mouth of books and the mouth of authors, which is the straight path a person should choose. And every single day he shall take in his hand the text of the great confession, and if he does not understand the holy tongue, let him go to a sage to write for him in the vernacular all the fine details of the sins that people stumble into. And every matter of transgression he sees he has stumbled into until now, let him accept upon himself with all firmness to abandon his evil way and make a fence for himself not to return again to folly. And Torah study outweighs them all, so let him accept upon himself with all firmness that at every time he is free, he shall free himself to study or go to a sage to have him teach him, for great is study that leads to action (Kiddushin 40b). And whatever he accepts upon himself to do good and withdraw his hand from doing every evil, let him write it down, and fine himself with a monetary fine, or some affliction and mortification, every time he transgresses and does not do as he accepted, and this reminder shall be a remembrance between his eyes, and he shall read it every single week and not transgress, for this is a great fence (as I have written above under the entry "Gader" [fence]).
Pele Yoetz 185:8: And day by day from Rosh Chodesh Elul onward, let him go on increasing and growing in the ways of repentance, and every day let him pour out his speech, seek forgiveness, and increase charity according to his ability, and wrap himself like a poor man and pour out his speech before the LORD, that He help him for the sake of the honor of His Name. And if he does not understand the holy tongue, let him go to a sage to arrange for him some text of confession and supplication in the vernacular, or to copy for him from the awesome prayers, of which there are books translated from the holy tongue into the vernacular. And when the eve of Yom Kippur arrives, let him add fear to his fear, for the day of the LORD is near, the great and awesome day of judgment. And at the morning watch, in the darkness of dawn, let him do as is the custom of Israel, to perform kapparot for all the members of the household, from the smallest to the greatest, for there is a secret in the matter, to sweeten the harsh judgments. And as they said in the plain meaning of the reason for the sacrifice, that it is so that his heart be humbled by considering that everything done to the animal would have been fitting to be done to him for his sin - so now let him intend that what he does to the rooster corresponds to the four death penalties: that holding it by the neck is like strangulation, the slaughter is like killing, casting it after slaughter is like stoning, and singeing it in fire is like burning. And let his heart be humbled by considering that this is what would have been fitting to be done to him, and let him pour out his speech, that it be considered as though it were done to himself (and I have made it my custom to say a text of prayer - this is its text):
Pele Yoetz 185:9: For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah: behold, I am ready and prepared to fulfill the custom of Israel to slaughter kapparot upon myself and upon the members of my household. May it be Your will, LORD our God and God of our fathers, that You have mercy on us, and reckon it for us as though we had done all that is incumbent upon us to do, and as though we had intended all the intentions proper to intend, and let the harsh judgments be sweetened, and draw kindnesses upon us, and let everything done to these fowl be considered as though it were done to ourselves, and reckon it for us as though we had been stoned, burned, killed, and strangled in the great court in Jerusalem through the four letters of Adnut [the Divine Name], and let what we have blemished in the twelve letters of the three precious Names, YHVH, EHYH, Adnut, be repaired, and let all the Names be unified in a complete unification, and let all the worlds be completely repaired, and let everything return to its original state, and let no one banished remain banished from Him. And let these fowl be the ransom of our souls, man for man, wood for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, and let this be my exchange, this my substitute, this my atonement (three times).
Pele Yoetz 185:10: This rooster shall go to death, and I shall enter into a good and long life and peace, for Your service and Your fear. Remember us for life, O King who desires life, write us in the book of life for Your sake, O living God. Please, merciful and gracious God, slow to anger - extend Your patience until we return to You in complete repentance before You, and do not take us from this world until we complete the repair of our nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, and hasten and speed our redemption, and build our Temple and our splendor, and there we shall offer sacrifices before You, and perform the ordinance of the scapegoat sent forth to atone for us, and You, in Your great mercy, shall desire us and be pleased with us. "And let it be pleasant," and so on. "Rejoice, the soul of Your servant, for to You, O LORD, I lift up my soul." "My God, in You I have trusted, let me not be ashamed." "Act for the sake of Your great mercies," and so on.
Pele Yoetz 185:11: And afterward let him give the fowl or their value to poor students of Torah and worthy men. And it is likewise customary to perform the order of the annulment of vows and the annulment of curses, and many of those who fear the LORD are accustomed to receive four lashes. And whoever's own hand does much to perform good customs and matters of piety during these days is praiseworthy, for this is what we seek: that the LORD our God enter with us in the attribute of kindness and the attribute of mercy, and enter with us beyond the letter of the law, for woe, who could live if the LORD were to establish the earth in strict judgment? And as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 143:2): "do not enter into judgment with Your servant, for no living being shall be justified before You." Therefore one must also increase in charity and kindness during these days, so that the LORD too perform charity and kindness with us, and overlook very, very much according to His own measures, so that the LORD too overlook transgression.
Pele Yoetz 185:12: And although it is very good to afflict oneself during these days as much as one can bear, for the hour requires this, in any case, when the eve of Yom Kippur arrives, the mitzvah of the day is to increase in eating and drinking as much as one can with fear, love, and great joy, as the living take to heart: what is accomplished in the heavens above through our eating on this day, which is a thing that stands at the height of the world and builds its chambers in heaven, and everything done through us, whether the eating on this day or the afflictions and prayers of Yom Kippur, is all a ladder set on the earth with its top reaching to heaven, and these matters are ancient. Happy is the one born of woman who merits this, happy is he who gives peace of mind to his Former, the King, high and exalted. And according to the plain meaning of the matter too, Israel shall rejoice in its Maker on this day with great joy unlike any other, for having sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us in the mitzvah of repentance, and before the wound He prepares the remedy, and He has said to us, "when you rebel against Me, take words with you and return to the LORD" (Hosea 14:3), for I am gracious, always reconciled through mercy and appeased through supplications, all the days, and especially "in the seventh month, on the tenth of the month, you shall afflict your souls, for on this day He shall atone for you" (Leviticus 16:30). And He commanded us in the Torah to afflict our souls only one day a year, and even this, out of the LORD's love for His people, He commanded us to precede it on the ninth day by increasing in eating, as a father does for a beloved son, saying to him, "eat much, my beloved son, so that you have strength to fast" - so did the LORD do for His chosen people, His firstborn son, and it shall be counted a mitzvah for us, both the eating and the afflictions and the prayers and the repentance, and He establishes for us good reward for them. Is there any palate sweeter than this? Happy are we, how good is our portion - it is impossible not to rejoice. And in any case, if regarding all the days it is said (Psalms 2:11), "and rejoice with trembling," all the more so on this day.
Pele Yoetz 185:13: Therefore he should not increase in drinking wine, and the wise man has his eyes in his head - let him increase eating in the morning in a manner that he have time for the food in his stomach to digest, and let his body be purified while it is still day, and after his meal let him lie down and rest a little so that he have the strength to stand guard on the night of Yom Kippur and on the mighty day, and then let him go back to his business, if he has any business. And let him purify himself within and without, that he relieve himself and purify his body in a purifying mikveh for the sake of repentance, and not transgress, and let him precede this with prayer and thoughts of repentance, and afterward pray the afternoon prayer while it is still broad daylight, and put on white garments and recline at his table while it is still broad daylight to eat the concluding meal, in a manner that he have time to proceed unhurriedly and that the food in his stomach settle before he goes to the synagogue. And let his food at the concluding meal be small in quantity and great in quality, such as good soup and a little poultry meat, and afterward let him be clothed in dread and go to the synagogue in awe, in fear, with trembling and sweat, to receive the sanctification of the mighty and awesome day.
